Helicoverpa zea: Same caterpillar, many names: corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, cotton bollworm, depending on what it is eating.
Helicoverpa armigera: A caterpillar with almost no dietary rules: it has been recorded on well over 100 plant species.
Spodoptera frugiperda: Fall armyworm caterpillars are cannibals; crowd them into one corn whorl and often only a few survive.
Spodoptera exigua: The beet armyworm is not loyal to beets; it eats a long list of vegetable and field crops.
Spodoptera eridania: Young southern armyworms often feed together in clusters before scattering as they grow.
Ostrinia nubilalis: The European corn borer likely reached the US around 1910 hidden in imported broomcorn.
Agrotis ipsilon: Black cutworm moths can ride spring storm winds north from the Gulf states into the Corn Belt.
Plutella xylostella: The diamondback moth has resisted so many insecticides that it is a textbook case of resistance evolution.
Trichoplusia ni: Cells from the cabbage looper (the 'High Five' line) are used in labs to make proteins.
Pieris rapae: The small white butterfly reached Quebec in the 1860s and now follows cabbage across North America.
Chrysodeixis includens: Soybean loopers walk by looping: they arch their backs like tiny green inchworms.
Anticarsia gemmatalis: A disturbed velvetbean caterpillar may thrash about and drop off the plant.
Manduca sexta: Hornworm moths hover at flowers like hummingbirds, and the caterpillar is a lab model for insect biology.
Pectinophora gossypiella: The pink bollworm hides inside cotton bolls; the US declared it eradicated from cotton in 2018.
Cydia pomonella: That 'worm in the apple' is often a codling moth caterpillar.
Aspila molesta: Orchards can be filled with synthetic female scent so male moths get confused and cannot find mates.
Phthorimaea absoluta: The tomato leafminer was reported in Spain in 2006 and has since traveled across Africa and Asia.
Diatraea saccharalis: In Brazil, tiny parasitoid wasps are released over large areas of sugarcane to control the sugarcane borer.
Chilo suppressalis: Rice stem borer damage has a dramatic name: 'deadheart', when the central shoot of a young rice plant dies.
Leptinotarsa decemlineata: The Colorado potato beetle switched from a wild nightshade to potatoes in the 1800s, then went on a world tour.
Diabrotica virgifera: Some rootworm populations evolved to lay eggs in soybean fields, outsmarting corn-soybean rotation.
Diabrotica undecimpunctata: Its Latin name says 'eleven-spotted', but the adult actually has twelve spots.
Anthonomus grandis: Enterprise, Alabama has a monument to the boll weevil, thanking it for pushing farmers to diversify.
Cerotoma trifurcata: Bean leaf beetles come in several colors and spot patterns, which makes ID a good challenge.
Epilachna varivestis: The Mexican bean beetle is a lady beetle relative that eats plants instead of aphids: the family black sheep.
Phyllotreta striolata: Flea beetles jump like fleas thanks to enlarged hind legs.
Psylliodes chrysocephala: Despite the 'flea' in its name it is a beetle, and it jumps with big hind legs.
Brassicogethes aeneus: Pollen beetles love yellow: an oilseed rape field can host thousands.
Sitona lineatus: Pea leaf weevils leave scalloped notches on leaf edges, like someone with tiny scissors.
Oulema melanopus: Cereal leaf beetle larvae cover themselves in their own droppings as protection.
Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus: Rice water weevil larvae live in flooded paddies, getting air from rice roots.
Popillia japonica: Japanese beetles were first found in the US in 1916, in a New Jersey nursery.
Conotrachelus nenuphar: Plum curculio females cut a little crescent-shaped scar in fruit to lay an egg.
Agriotes lineatus: Wireworms become click beetles, which flip themselves into the air with a click when upside down.
Sitophilus oryzae: A female rice weevil lays an egg inside a single grain kernel, then plugs the hole.
Tribolium castaneum: The red flour beetle was the first beetle to have its genome sequenced (2008).
Aphis glycines: First found in North America in 2000, the soybean aphid spread across the soybean belt within a few years.
Aphis gossypii: Cotton aphids range from pale yellow to nearly black depending on conditions.
Myzus persicae: A small bug with a big mailbag: the green peach aphid can transmit well over 100 plant viruses.
Rhopalosiphum padi: Bird cherry-oat aphids have two homes: bird cherry trees in winter, cereals in summer.
Rhopalosiphum maidis: Aphid mothers can give birth to daughters already carrying the embryos of granddaughters.
Sitobion avenae: Ants sometimes guard aphid colonies like tiny cattle and collect their honeydew.
Acyrthosiphon pisum: Pea aphids can be red or green, and some of their pigment genes were borrowed from fungi.
Bemisia tabaci: Bemisia tabaci is not one species but a complex of look-alike species.
Trialeurodes vaporariorum: Brush a greenhouse tomato plant and a cloud of tiny white 'flies' rises.
Diaphorina citri: Adult Asian citrus psyllids feed with their rear ends tilted up in the air.
Nilaparvata lugens: Heavy brown planthopper outbreaks cause 'hopperburn': rice patches that look scorched.
Empoasca fabae: Potato leafhoppers walk sideways, like tiny crabs.
Lygus lineolaris: The tarnished plant bug is named for its mottled look, like an old silver spoon.
Lygus hesperus: Lygus feeding can leave strawberries lumpy and misshapen; growers call it 'cat-facing'.
Halyomorpha halys: In autumn, brown marmorated stink bugs gather on house walls looking for a warm place to overwinter.
Nezara viridula: The southern green stink bug can turn brownish in cooler months.
Euschistus servus: Stink bugs 'stink' because of defensive chemicals released from scent glands.
Megacopta cribraria: The kudzu bug was first found in Georgia in 2009 and spread across the Southeast within a few years.
Murgantia histrionica: The harlequin bug wears a flashy orange-and-black costume.
Anasa tristis: Squash bug eggs sit in neat bronze clusters on the undersides of leaves.
Leptoglossus phyllopus: 'Leaf-footed' refers to the flattened, leaf-like expansions on the hind legs.
Lycorma delicatula: The spotted lanternfly is not a fly and does not glow: it is a planthopper.
Frankliniella occidentalis: 'Thrips' is both singular and plural: one thrips, two thrips.
Thrips tabaci: Onion thrips are only 1-2 mm long, but their silvery feeding scars are easy to spot.
Tetranychus urticae: Spider mites are not spiders, but they do spin silk webs on leaves.
Drosophila suzukii: Most fruit flies wait for rotting fruit; this one has a saw-like egg-layer and uses ripe fruit.
Ceratitis capitata: Programs release millions of sterile male medflies to keep wild populations in check.
Bactrocera dorsalis: Males are irresistibly attracted to methyl eugenol, a plant compound used in traps.
Delia radicum: Gardeners put little collars around cabbage seedlings to stop this fly laying eggs.
Melanoplus differentialis: The differential grasshopper has black herringbone marks on its hind legs.
Locusta migratoria: Crowded locusts change color, shape and behavior: a shy grasshopper becomes a swarmer.
Schistocerca gregaria: A desert locust can eat roughly its own weight in plants each day.
Solenopsis invicta: Fire ants survive floods by linking together into living rafts.
Hippodamia convergens: The 'convergent' lady beetle is named for two white lines on its thorax that converge.
Harmonia axyridis: When threatened, Asian lady beetles 'reflex bleed' a smelly yellow fluid from their leg joints.
Coccinella septempunctata: The 'lady' in ladybird is often said to refer to the Virgin Mary.
Adalia bipunctata: The two-spot ladybird comes as red with black spots or black with red spots, same species.
Coleomegilla maculata: This ladybird eats pollen as well as aphids and insect eggs: a flexible diet.
Chrysoperla carnea: Green lacewing larvae are nicknamed 'aphid lions'.
Chrysoperla rufilabris: Lacewing eggs sit on tiny silk stalks, away from hungry siblings.
Orius insidiosus: Tiny but bold: the minute pirate bug eats thrips, mites and insect eggs.
Geocoris punctipes: Big-eyed bugs look permanently startled, but they are hungry predators of eggs and small insects.
Nabis roseipennis: Damsel bugs ambush prey with grasping front legs, despite the delicate name.
Podisus maculiventris: Rare among stink bugs, the spined soldier bug is a caterpillar-eating good guy.
Perillus bioculatus: A stink bug that eats Colorado potato beetle larvae: a grower's friend.
Zelus longipes: Assassin bugs inject saliva that liquefies prey from the inside.
Calosoma scrutator: Its common name is 'fiery searcher': a glittering caterpillar-hunting ground beetle.
Pterostichus melanarius: This ground beetle works the night shift, eating slugs, weed seeds and insects.
Poecilus cupreus: 'Cupreus' means coppery, and it gleams like a new penny.
Harpalus pensylvanicus: Its species name spells Pennsylvania with one 'n', an older spelling.
Aleochara bilineata: Its larvae hunt cabbage root fly pupae and sneak right inside the puparium.
Cotesia congregata: Hornworms covered in white cocoons look sprinkled with rice; those are wasp cocoons.
Aphidius ervi: Parasitized aphids turn into golden 'mummies', and the wasp cuts a round exit hole.
Trichopoda pennipes: Feather-legged flies glue eggs onto stink bugs, which then carry them around.
Toxomerus politus: Hover flies dress like wasps but cannot sting: all fashion, no risk.
Allograpta obliqua: Hover flies can hover in place and even fly backward.
Episyrphus balteatus: Marmalade hoverflies migrate across Europe in huge numbers.
Forficula auricularia: Despite the ear myth, earwig mothers guard their eggs and tend their young.
Pardosa milvina: Wolf spider mothers carry their egg sacs, then their spiderlings on their backs.
Oxyopes salticus: Lynx spiders pounce on prey like tiny cats.
Phidippus audax: Jumping spiders have excellent vision for their size, and bold jumpers will stare right back.
Phytoseiulus persimilis: Predatory mites are sold by mail order and shaken from a bottle onto plants.
Neoseiulus californicus: A mini-predator that can switch to pollen when spider mites are scarce.
Apis mellifera: A worker honey bee makes only about 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.
Bombus impatiens: Bumble bees 'buzz-pollinate': they vibrate flowers to shake pollen loose, a trick tomatoes love.
Bombus terrestris: Bumble bees warm up by shivering their flight muscles, so they can fly on cool days.
Bombus vosnesenskii: The yellow-faced bumble bee is named for the Russian naturalist Ilya Voznesensky.
Bombus bimaculatus: Each spring a lone bumble bee queen starts a whole colony from scratch.
Osmia lignaria: Blue orchard bees nest in hollow tunnels and seal each cell with mud.
Osmia bicornis: Red mason bees move into 'bee hotels' made of hollow tubes.
Osmia cornifrons: Japanese farmers have used the hornfaced bee in apple orchards for decades.
Megachile rotundata: Alfalfa leafcutting bees cut circular leaf pieces for their nests, like tiny hole punchers.
Nomia melanderi: Alkali bees nest in dense 'bee cities' on alkaline soil flats.
Xenoglossa pruinosa: Squash bees are early birds, visiting squash flowers at dawn; males nap inside the flowers.
Habropoda laboriosa: 'Laboriosa' means hardworking, and this blueberry bee lives up to it.
Agapostemon virescens: Sweat bees are sometimes drawn to the salt in human sweat.
Melissodes bimaculatus: Male longhorn bees sleep clinging to plant stems by their jaws.
Eristalis tenax: The drone fly's 'rat-tailed' maggot breathes through a telescopic snorkel.
Danaus plexippus: Monarch migration spans generations: no single butterfly makes the whole round trip.
Daphnia magna: Water fleas are transparent, so you can watch the heart beat under a microscope.
Daphnia pulex: Daphnia pulex was one of the first crustaceans to have its genome sequenced.
Chironomus riparius: Midge larvae are called 'bloodworms' because hemoglobin turns them red.
Gammarus fasciatus: Scuds like this amphipod often swim on their sides.
Chironomus dilutus: Adult midges do not bite, and most barely feed: the party is in the larval stage.
Gammarus pulex: Freshwater shrimp are shredders: they turn fallen leaves into stream food.
Hexagenia limbata: Hexagenia mayfly hatches are so big they show up on weather radar.
Cloeon dipterum: Unlike most mayflies, this one gives birth to live young.
Pteronarcys californica: Anglers wait for the giant 'salmonfly hatch' because trout go wild for it.
Eisenia fetida: Called 'tiger worms' for their stripes, red wigglers turn food scraps to compost at an impressive rate.
Lumbricus terrestris: Darwin's last book was about earthworms, and it sold well.
Folsomia candida: This springtail is eyeless, white and reproduces without males.
Armadillidium vulgare: Pill bugs are crustaceans, land-living cousins of shrimp, not insects.
Drosophila melanogaster: Fruit flies have flown in space, and their research has contributed to several Nobel Prizes.
Lumbriculus variegatus: Cut a blackworm in two and each piece can regrow into a whole worm.
Striacosta albicosta: Despite its name, corn is a main host of the western bean cutworm in much of the Corn Belt.
Melanaphis sacchari: Aphid math: females reproduce without mating, so populations can balloon in weeks.
Piezodorus guildinii: The reddish band across its back is the redbanded stink bug's giveaway.
Chloridea virescens: The tobacco budworm is also called the geranium budworm for its taste in flowers.
Novius cardinalis: Named for its cardinal-red color, the vedalia beetle is a very small hero of citrus.
Trissolcus japonicus: The samurai wasp is only a few millimeters long, yet it takes on stink bug eggs.
Melipona quadrifasciata: Stingless bees cannot sting, but some will crawl into your hair and bite.
Pimephales promelas: Male fathead minnows guard the eggs like dedicated dads.
Lemna minor: Duckweed is a flowering plant that rarely flowers: it mostly clones itself.
Ceriodaphnia dubia: Water flea mothers can make clonal babies without mating, so lab cultures stay consistent.
Varroa destructor: Varroa is named after the Roman author Varro, who wrote about bees.
Photinus pyralis: 'Femme fatale' fireflies (Photuris) mimic its flashes to lure and eat the males.
Brachinus fumans: Bombardier beetles fire a hot, pulsing chemical spray: a tiny jet engine.
